definition: Analgesic means a substance that relieves pain.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word analgesic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know analgesic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After the dental surgery, the oral surgeon recommended an over-the-counter analgesic to manage the soreness.
A balm merely soothes minor discomfort, while an analgesic actively relieves real pain.
An anesthetic goes further than an analgesic — it blocks sensation entirely rather than just easing pain.

A painkiller is any drug that relieves pain, and it is the everyday word — the one you use at home or hear across a drugstore counter. Analgesic names exactly the same kind of drug in clinical language: the term printed on medicine labels and written on charts. The difference is register, not meaning.

Pain reliever is the gentle phrase printed on over-the-counter boxes for a medicine that eases aches — plain words chosen to reassure shoppers. An analgesic is the same medicine under its technical name, the word a pharmacist or a research paper would choose. Say pain reliever in the aisle; write analgesic on the chart.

One bar of the old summer-camp song was enough to fill the counselors with nostalgia.
Analgesic means a substance that relieves pain.
By mile twenty, Priya's knees throbbed with every stride.
At the finish-line medical tent, a volunteer offered her ice and a mild analgesic.
Within an hour the sharp ache had faded to a dull background hum.
Nothing about the pill fixed her knees — it simply quieted the pain they were sending.
The pill relieves Priya's pain without curing or treating anything else — doing exactly and only what an analgesic does.
You'll meet analgesic on medicine labels and in doctors' offices.

Keep it apart from antiseptic (another word in this unit): an analgesic relieves pain, while antiseptic describes something that prevents infection by keeping germs away — a well-stocked first-aid kit needs both, because neither does the other's job.

Long before pharmacies, people chewed willow bark when their joints ached.
They could not have named the chemistry, but they had found a genuine analgesic.
The bark's bitter compound, salicin, dulls pain without putting the patient to sleep — relief, not unconsciousness.
In the nineteenth century, chemists learned first to isolate the compound and then to tame it, softening a molecule that had been hard on the stomach.
The result, sold as aspirin, became the most widely taken drug on earth.
Its job description never changed: quiet the pain and otherwise leave the body alone.
Modern successors crowd the shelves, but they are judged by the old bark's standard — how much hurt they remove, and how little else they disturb.
